flagDescription: The Kenyan flag is a horizontal tricolor of black, red and green, separated by thin white stripes. Red

White

Maasai shield

flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Japan is a white rectangle with a large crimson circle in the center, representing the sun. It is known as the Hinomaru, meaning 'circle of the sun'.
flagDescription: The Japanese flag is a white field with a crimson disc at its center, representing the sun. The diameter of the disc is three-fifths of the flag's height, and the flag proportion is 2:3. The design has been used unofficially since the 19th century and was formalized as the national flag by the Act on National Flag and Anthem in 1999.
flagColors: WhiteCrimson
colorMeaningSummary: White represents purity and honesty, and the crimson disc represents the sun, reflecting Japan's name — 'Land of the Rising Sun'. The design has deep cultural roots and was historically used on banners by samurai and during the Meiji period.
colorMeaningDetailed:
White

Represents purity, honesty and integrity — a value central to Japanese aesthetics and Shinto tradition.

Crimson

Represents sincerity, warmth and the sun itself. The specific shade used today is a bright, slightly pinkish red specified by the 1999 law.

Hinomaru (sun disc)

The red circle represents the rising sun, an ancient symbol of Japan and its imperial lineage. The name 'Japan' in Chinese characters (日本) literally means 'origin of the sun'.

Proportions

The 1999 law set the disc diameter to three-fifths of the flag's height, larger than many pre-modern versions of the Hinomaru.
flagHistory: The Hinomaru has been used in Japan since at least the 7th century, when it appeared on banners and court decorations. During the Edo period it was used on merchant ships, and in 1870 the Meiji government designated it for use on Japanese vessels. It served as the de facto national flag throughout the imperial era, but was only formally codified as the national flag on 13 August 1999 with the Act on National Flag and Anthem. The 1999 law also fixed the disc's proportions and the exact shade of red.
flagDesigner: Unknown — traditional design formalized by the Meiji government
similarFlagsAnswer: Bangladesh also uses a red disc, but on a green field and offset toward the hoist. Palau uses a yellow disc on a light blue field. Japan's white-and-red design is otherwise unique.

  • Japan Self-Defense Forces flag (1954–present): A modern version with adjusted proportions.
  • Meiji-era merchant flag: A smaller-disc Hinomaru used on civilian vessels before 1999.

flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Brazil has a green background, a yellow rhombus in the center, and a blue circle with 27 white stars and a white band reading 'Ordem e Progresso' ('Order and Progress').
flagDescription: The Brazilian flag consists of a green rectangle, a yellow rhombus centered on it, and a blue circle with white stars and a white equatorial band bearing the national motto 'Ordem e Progresso'. The flag proportion is 7:10. It was adopted on 19 November 1889, four days after the proclamation of the republic, and its current form (with 27 stars) dates from 1992.
flagColors: GreenYellowBlueWhite
colorMeaningSummary: Green represents the House of Braganza and Brazil's forests, yellow represents the House of Habsburg and the country's gold, and blue represents the sky over Rio de Janeiro on the morning of 15 November 1889. The 27 stars represent the 26 states and the Federal District, and the motto 'Ordem e Progresso' is inspired by Auguste Comte's positivism.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Green

Represents the forests of Brazil and the House of Braganza, the imperial dynasty that ruled Brazil until 1889.

Yellow

Represents Brazil's gold reserves and the House of Habsburg, to which Empress Maria Leopoldina belonged.

Blue

Represents the sky over Rio de Janeiro on 15 November 1889, the day the republic was proclaimed. The stars are arranged as seen from that location at that moment.

White

Used for the stars, the motto band and the border of the rhombus — representing peace and purity.

Stars

There are 27 stars — one for each state plus the Federal District. Nine star sizes correspond to the states' sizes on the actual Brazilian sky.

Ordem e Progresso

The motto means 'Order and Progress' and is derived from Auguste Comte's positivist slogan 'L'amour pour principe et l'ordre pour base; le progrès pour but'.
flagHistory: The Brazilian flag was adopted on 19 November 1889 by decree of the provisional republican government, four days after the monarchy was overthrown. It was designed by Raimundo Teixeira Mendes, Miguel Lemos, Manuel Pereira Reis and Décio Villares, drawing on the flag of the earlier Empire of Brazil (green field, yellow rhombus, imperial coat of arms). The republican design replaced the coat of arms with a blue celestial globe. The flag has been updated several times as new states were created — the most recent change added a 27th star in 1992.
flagDesigner: Raimundo Teixeira Mendes, Miguel Lemos, Manuel Pereira Reis, Décio Villares
similarFlagsAnswer: The Brazilian flag is unique among national flags for its astronomical globe. No other country's flag is closely comparable.
flagVariants:

  • Empire of Brazil (1822–1889): Green field, yellow rhombus, imperial coat of arms in the center.
  • Republic (1889–1960): The current design with 21 stars, adding one per new state over time.
  • Republic (1960–1992): 22 stars after the creation of Guanabara and later the Federal District.
  • Current version (1992–present): 27 stars, matching the current federal units.

The design uses six colors — black, green, yellow, white, red and blue — making it one of the most colorful national flags in the world.

flagHistory: The South African flag was designed by Frederick Brownell, then State Herald of South Africa, and adopted on 27 April 1994 — the day of the first democratic elections following the end of apartheid. The design combines colors from both the pre-1994 flag (orange, white, blue) and the ANC flag (black, green, yellow), deliberately avoiding any direct reference to either side of the apartheid conflict.

flagSubtitle: Three horizontal bands of black, red and gold — the Schwarz-Rot-Gold of the 1848 revolution.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Germany is a horizontal tricolor of black, red and gold (golden yellow) in three equal bands.
flagDescription: The German flag consists of three equal horizontal bands of black, red and gold. The flag proportion is 3:5. It was adopted in its current form on 23 May 1949 for West Germany and retained after reunification in 1990. The colors trace back to the uniforms of the Lützow Free Corps during the Napoleonic Wars and became the symbol of the 1848 German revolution.
flagColors: BlackRedGold
colorMeaningSummary: The colors originated with the Lützow Free Corps during the Napoleonic Wars and became the symbol of the 1848 German revolution and the struggle for a unified, democratic Germany. Black represents determination and dignity, red represents bravery and hardiness, and gold represents generosity and the aspiration for freedom and unity.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Black

Represents determination, dignity and, historically, the dark uniforms of the Lützow Free Corps.

Red

Represents bravery, hardiness and the blood shed in the struggle for German unity.

Gold

Represents generosity, freedom and the golden buttons on the Free Corps' uniforms. Officially a golden yellow, not a metallic gold.

Origin (1813)

The Lützow Free Corps — a volunteer unit during the Napoleonic Wars — wore black uniforms with red trim and gold buttons. Members popularized the color combination on their return to civilian life.

1848 revolution

The Frankfurt Parliament adopted black-red-gold as the flag of a unified German state, cementing its association with liberal and democratic ideals.
flagHistory: The black-red-gold tricolor was first adopted by the Frankfurt Parliament in 1848 as the flag of a unified, democratic Germany. The Weimar Republic (1919–1933) used it as the national flag. The Nazi regime replaced it with a red flag bearing a swastika from 1933 to 1945. After World War II, both West Germany (1949) and East Germany (1949) adopted the black-red-gold tricolor. East Germany added a hammer-and-compass emblem in 1959, which West Germany considered a violation of the shared flag. On 3 October 1990, reunification restored the plain tricolor as the flag of a single Germany.
flagDesigner: Unknown — derived from the Lützow Free Corps uniforms
similarFlagsAnswer: Belgium uses vertical black-yellow-red bands, and the Netherlands uses horizontal red-white-blue. Germany is the only country with horizontal black-red-gold.
flagVariants:

Germany has had several national flags across different political eras. The black-red-gold tricolor is not the only design the country has used.

  • German Empire (1871–1918): Black-white-red horizontal tricolor.
  • Weimar Republic (1919–1933): Black-red-gold tricolor.
  • Nazi Germany (1933–1945): Red flag with a black swastika on a white disc.
  • East Germany (1949–1990): Black-red-gold with a hammer, compass and ring of rye.
  • West Germany (1949–1990): Plain black-red-gold tricolor.
  • Reunified Germany (1990–present): Plain black-red-gold tricolor.

flagSubtitle: Three vertical bands of blue, white and red — the Tricolore, symbol of the French Revolution.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of France is a vertical tricolor of blue, white and red in three equal bands. It is known as the Tricolore.
flagDescription: The French flag consists of three equal vertical bands of blue (hoist), white (center) and red (fly). The proportion is 2:3. It was adopted on 15 February 1794 during the French Revolution and has remained the national flag ever since, with only brief interruptions in 1814–1830 and 1848.
flagColors: BlueWhiteRed
colorMeaningSummary: Blue and red are the traditional colors of Paris, worn by the militia that stormed the Bastille in 1789. White was the color of the Bourbon monarchy. Combined, they represent the union of the people and the crown under the new republic — and are popularly said to stand for liberty, equality and fraternity.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Blue

The traditional color of Paris, associated with Saint Martin and the city's militia. Often linked to liberty.

White

The color of the Bourbon monarchy and the royal standard of France before the Revolution. Placed between blue and red, it represents peace and the reconciliation of the nation.

Red

The traditional color of Paris, associated with Saint Denis and the revolutionary flag of 1789. Often linked to equality and the blood of the revolution.

Liberty, Equality, Fraternity

The popular association of blue, white and red with the national motto is a 19th-century interpretation, not part of the original design.
flagHistory: The Tricolore emerged during the French Revolution. On 13 July 1789, the day before the storming of the Bastille, Parisian militia adopted a cockade of blue and red — the city's colors. On 17 July, Lafayette added white to create a national cockade combining the colors of Paris with the royal white. A flag based on this cockade was adopted by the National Convention on 15 February 1794. It was briefly replaced during the Bourbon Restoration (1814–1830) and the Second Republic (1848), but has been the national flag continuously since 1830.
flagDesigner: Lafayette (cockade origin)
similarFlagsAnswer: The Netherlands and Luxembourg also use vertical blue-white-red tricolors, but with different proportions and shades. France's blue is darker and Luxembourg's blue is lighter.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

France has changed its national flag several times, and the Tricolore itself has been used in several configurations.

  • Kingdom of France (pre-1789): White flag with golden fleurs-de-lis.
  • Bourbon Restoration (1814–1830): Plain white flag.
  • July Monarchy (1830–1848): Tricolore with a restored cockade.
  • Second Republic (1848): Briefly red flag considered, then Tricolore retained.
  • Vichy France (1940–1944): Tricolore with a Francisque emblem.
  • Free France (1940–1944): Tricolore with a red Cross of Lorraine.

White

Red

flagHistory: The Italian tricolor was first adopted by the Cispadane Republic on 7 January 1797, in Reggio Emilia, based on the French Tricolore with green replacing blue. The Kingdom of Italy adopted it in 1861 with the royal Savoy coat of arms in the center. When Italy became a republic in 1946, the coat of arms was removed, and the plain tricolor was formally adopted on 1 January 1948.
flagDesigner: Giuseppe Compagnoni (Cispadane Republic)

flagHistory: The red-yellow-red design was chosen by King Charles III in 1785 to distinguish Spanish naval ships from those of other nations, which used similar white ensigns.
